prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators have the structure I look for: a simple, general mechanism (the Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states) that is analytically transparent and was then tested in a decisive experiment (HgTe quantum wells). The idea has travelled well beyond solid-state physics into photonics, cold atoms and acoustics, which is the kind of universality I value. It is independently confirmed in several material systems over fifteen to twenty years, so the maturity question is settled, and it enjoys the broadest opening support among the theory-led candidates (five ranked it, three in their top three). After reading the ballots I move it ahead of my own opening first choice, B011, mainly because the support for B011 is only mine and I cannot honestly argue that my enthusiasm for an analytically clean model should outweigh a field-wide verdict.
statement.case_against: The credited trio leaves out a pivotal step. The HgTe quantum-well prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what made the Molenkamp experiment possible, and the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) is a separate, partly competing story; Kane-Mele's graphene proposal is also not the system in which the effect was finally seen, because spin-orbit gaps in graphene are tiny. The 2016 prize on topological phases adds a possible overlap objection. If the committee concludes that the three-person limit cannot represent this history fairly, I would rather lose this configuration than award it on a distorted record.

responses.point: B049 is a new state of matter with a clean theory-plus-experiment story (Kane and Mele for the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal, Molenkamp for HgTe edge transport), confirmed in many laboratories and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the maturity. Where I would qualify your account is attribution. Calling it a clean trio treats Molenkamp's experiment as the realisation of Kane-Mele, but it realised the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, and Kane and Mele's graphene mechanism was not what was observed. I think the citation therefore has to be worded around the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators as a concept and a first observation, not around a single lineage. I also doubt that one prize should absorb the 3D materials as well, as you suggest as a possibility. Splitting 2D and 3D would not fit within the person limit, so I would keep the 2D citation and accept that the 3D discoverers are left out.

responses.point: B008 is the top-ranked candidate: the optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength idea with Ye's record accuracy, is mature, and the attribution is clean, while B049 suffers from a genuine attribution problem with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: I take your attribution point on B049 seriously and share it, which is why I list the omission as my main reservation. But I do not think a clean attribution is by itself an argument for B008. The lattice clock is an outstanding, mature measurement advance, and I would be content with it as the alternative. My difficulty is the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems, which you and Kroll both acknowledge. Is the novelty of the lattice clock a new physical principle (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms to beat the quantum projection noise limit) or a very large improvement in an established technology? I would like to hear that argued from the atomic-physics side before I accept that attribution cleanliness decides it.

responses.point: B049 is strongly influential and confirmed, but the omission of Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes, Moore, Fu and Hasan is a real attribution problem, the quantised edge-transport evidence is more delicate than the topology concept, and it overlaps with the 2016 topological-phase prize.
responses.response: I agree with the delicacy of the edge transport: the HgTe conductance plateaus are a robust result, but nonlocal and long-edge measurements are less clean than the textbook picture, and that is a fair experimental caveat. On the 2016 overlap I would answer that the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall-type phases (TKNN-class, Haldane), whereas the Z2 class and time-reversal-protected edge states are a different symmetry-class concept, so I do not see it as a repeat. I also note that your own first choice, B012, was explicitly flagged by you and by Kroll as possibly too close to the 2025 circuits prize. I would not treat that proximity as disqualifying, but it argues for waiting rather than moving it to the top now.

responses.point: B008 is the right kind of measurement advance, with Katori and Ye the clean pair, and the main questions are whether the 2005 comb and ion-clock prizes already cover the area and whether to wait for the SI second redefinition.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition, since the physics is already secure. My reservation about B008 is a matter of weighing, not a defect: it is primarily an advance in measurement precision whose new physics (tests of constants, redshift at millimetre scale) is still prospective, while B049 already changed how a whole community thinks about electronic phases. I would not call that a decisive argument, and I could vote for B008 without discomfort.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp configuration given that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) and the 3D topological insulator discoverers are not credited, and whether the citation wording can avoid misstating the lineage.
Whether the 2016 topological-phase prize makes a topological insulator prize look like a repeat to the wider committee and Academy.

Whether B011 (KPZ universality) can be made fair: Parisi's omission, the role of the exact-solution mathematicians (Tracy-Widom connection, exact solutions of the KPZ equation) and the dominance of one liquid-crystal experiment are all unresolved, and I am the only member who ranked it.
Whether a technology-heavy candidate such as B008 should be valued above a concept-driven one on equal footing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any of the shortlisted candidates or their credited names. As a general note, I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), whose preferred areas (circuit QED, aberration-corrected electron microscopy) are on the shortlist; I have no specific collaboration with them and do not think it requires recusal.
